plan.contextChunk: This figure consists of one large unit circle annotated with the standard special angles and the coordinates of their terminal points. A heavy black circle is centered on thin horizontal and vertical axes, and sixteen straight radii run from the center out to filled dots placed every 30 or 45 degrees around the circumference. Each dot carries an external label in two colors: the angle written in degrees and then in radians in red, followed by the point's (x, y) coordinates in black. Reading counterclockwise from the right, the labels begin 0 degrees, 0, (1, 0), with 360 degrees, 2pi, (1, 0) printed directly beneath it, then 30 degrees, pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, 1/2); 45 degrees, pi/4, (sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2); 60 degrees, pi/3, (1/2, sqrt(3)/2); and 90 degrees, pi/2, (0, 1) at the top. The second quadrant continues with 120, 135, and 150 degrees and closes at 180 degrees, pi, (-1, 0); the third runs 210, 225, and 240 degrees to 270 degrees, 3pi/2, (0, -1); and the fourth returns through 300 and 315 degrees to 330 degrees, 11pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, -1/2). The symmetric placement is the point of the layout, since the same three magnitudes 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, and sqrt(3)/2 recur in every quadrant with only their signs changing. Gathering all the major angles on one circle lets values outside the first quadrant be recovered by reflection rather than recomputed.

interactions.teaches: Each special angle has equivalent degree, radian, and coordinate descriptions, and points with the same reference angle reuse the same coordinate magnitudes with signs determined by quadrant.
A terminal point on the unit circle has coordinates (cos θ, sin θ), so the horizontal and vertical projections are the cosine and sine values for that angle.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Once you know the first-quadrant special-angle coordinates, every other standard unit-circle value follows by reflection and quadrant signs.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate a centered unit circle with a strong black circumference, thinner x- and y-axes with arrowheads, and sixteen radii to the standard 30-degree and 45-degree special-angle positions. Place filled black dots at each terminal point. Put angle labels in red and coordinate labels in black outside the circle, arranged symmetrically around the perimeter: 0/360 at the right, 90 at the top, 180 at the left, and 270 at the bottom. The three recurring coordinate magnitudes should be visually clear: 1/2, √2/2, and √3/2, with signs changing by quadrant. In hover mode, brighten the selected dot and its degree/radian/coordinate label while outlining the other points with the same reference angle. In click mode, emphasize the selected radius and draw projection segments from the terminal point to the axes, labeling the horizontal component as cos θ and the vertical component as sin θ. The label-mode toggle should hide nonselected label categories to reduce clutter while preserving the same dots and radii.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Hover for each terminal point: the learner points at a dot on the circle, its degree measure, radian measure, and coordinate label brighten while symmetric points with the same reference angle are outlined, making the repeated magnitudes and quadrant sign changes clear.
- Click for component projections: the learner clicks an angle ray, horizontal and vertical projection segments drop to the axes and the coordinate pair is rebuilt as (cos theta, sin theta), connecting the unit-circle point to the two trigonometric values.
- Toggle between degree, radian, and coordinate label modes: the learner switches the visible label set, reducing clutter while showing that all three descriptions refer to the same fixed terminal points.

authoredContext:
Now that we have learned how to find the cosine and sine values for special angles in the first quadrant, we can use symmetry and reference angles to fill in cosine and sine values for the rest of the special angles on the unit circle. They are shown in the figure. Take time to learn the (x,y) coordinates of all of the major angles in the first quadrant.

discrepancies: Several left-side red angle labels are clipped by the edge of the rendered figure, making labels such as 150° and 210° only partially visible.
The 0°/360° labels and the corresponding (1, 0) coordinate labels on the right overlap/crowd each other much more than in the source.
Many coordinate labels use plain inline slash notation such as √3/2 instead of the stacked fraction math formatting shown in the source, reducing visual fidelity and legibility.
The visible figure is scaled down and shifted left because the large control panel occupies the right side, so the default state is not a clean drop-in replacement for the static source image.
Several labels around the lower-right and upper-left quadrants are placed too close to the circle or to neighboring labels compared with the more spacious source layout.
The generated figure adds a prominent interactive UI panel not present in the source, which changes the overall composition even though the main unit-circle concept remains recognizable.
evaluation.notes: The unit-circle geometry, angles, coordinates, and colors are mostly correct, but the default rendered composition suffers from clipped/crowded labels and a large UI panel that prevents it from matching the source as a static figure.
action_items: Reposition the left-side labels farther inside the SVG viewBox or expand the left margin so no angle labels are clipped.
Separate the 0°/360° red labels from the two (1, 0) coordinate labels to match the source layout and avoid overlap.
Use stacked fraction-style math text or SVG tspans for coordinates and radian labels instead of plain slash notation.
Reduce or relocate the control panel so the default view preserves the full source-like unit circle layout at inline size.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are strong, but the issues are concrete rendering/layout problems—clipped and crowded labels, fraction formatting, scaling, and an intrusive control panel—that the generator can fix without changing the plan.
